utterances.text: When Karanovic returned he told us to pack our things, we were going to Blazevici, the command was there, he said, and that's where we would be interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the two of them, they escorted you, they didn't tie your hands behind your back; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: They didn't. They took us further on. We passed through a hamlet called Djukici after which the road went through the forest, where two other soldiers emerged. I asked my relatives who they were. And they answered that those were the Djukic brothers who lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we briefly look at 65 ter 22086? Would you please take a look at this page, page number 2? Oh, please get the page back, do get the Serbian version back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we ensure this isn't broadcast, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give this statement in our language and sign it? You see what it says there, in the meantime, on 28 June, Vlado Vrkes came?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We didn't get the answer from the witness to your previous question. What was your answer? Did you give this statement in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you say here that you did not know these two men who came with Vrkes, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: I didn't know Vrkes or the other two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Take a look at what it says here: "Vrkes was in a military uniform and I recognised him as soon as he arrived."

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: I don't know. It may be a mistake. I didn't know this Vrkes. Maybe I wasn't paying attention when I was reading this and signing it. But the fact remains that I did not know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So anyone could have said, "I'm Vrkes" and you would have accepted that because you had not known him from before?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: That could have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So then you were taken to the house, you say that you were taken by two criminals, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: No, I did not say criminals. These were two Serbs who lived in that village too. When we passed through those woods, then two other men got out, so there were four of them there ultimately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us look at page 2 of this same statement from 1996 where you say that there were two criminals, that's how you describe them.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: I can't find it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It should be page 2. Now, is it in e-court? Just a moment, please. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you referring to two local Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I was about to say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You characterised them as local Chetniks, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: For me, a Serb soldier who wears a cockade is a Chetnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They did wear cockade?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: One did and the other one had the tricolour flag on his uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You never mentioned the Tricolour flag until now.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then two more Chetniks joined them from Djukici, right? And you called them Chetniks, too, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Yes. One of them had a cockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So first there were two of them and then there were another two and they took you to Dujo Banovic's house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about Dujo Banovic, was he a Serb?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: I didn't know the man. He did not live in that house at that point in time. I think he was a Catholic, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dusan Banovic could hardly be a Catholic, Mr. Witness; isn't that right? It's a Serb name. First name and last name.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: I didn't say Dusan, I said Dujo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Isn't Dujo a term of endearment for Dusan?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: I don't know. I just know that that was the man's name. Dujo. And there was this other house there near that one, another man lived there, I don't know his name and I know that they were both Catholics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell us, then, how many of you walked into the house? You younger people. And how many older people sat outside?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Perhaps five younger persons entered the house. Some people were still standing by the entrance into the house, whereas these elderly people were still outside. I don't know how many of them there were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. They remained sitting outside. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: They were still outside. They had told us that we had to go inside and that they were cocking their rifles - whatever the word may be - and they pointed rifles at us and shade said that we had to go in. I was among the first people who went in these people stayed outside and they said, "Why do we have to go inside if we can stay outside. If you want to interrogate us you can go do that outdoors. You don't have to make us go inside."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say, we younger men went inside whereas the others sat outside in front of the house trying to persuade Djukic Rado and Mico to stay outside; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this discussion went on as they were sitting outside, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Once I walked in, I could not know whether they were still sitting outside or not, when they told us that we had to go into the house, they were still sitting out there and then when they told us we should go in, they stayed outside although we went in. And I don't know how long they stayed outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When was it that someone shouted, "Watch out, grenade"?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Perhaps two or three minutes had gone by.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where did the grenade come from?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: I don't know from where. Probably from outside, because you could hear it hit against the wooden boards, probably it came from the entrance door.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who was it that shouted, "Watch out, grenade"?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Probably those who were still standing by the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-hah. Whose grenade was that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Probably those Serbs who brought us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It couldn't have belonged to some Muslim?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How come you know that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Because no one had a grenade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you search them and thereby know that they did not have any grenades?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you say that you jumped out before the grenade exploded; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Three of you jumped out; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: I know that I jumped out and how many others did, I don't know. Later on, I think there was another man but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I can mention the name of the person who jumped out but you say that he fell and then you fell over him, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Yes. Once we jumped out of that house, it was about two or three metres down, and then this -- one of these Serbs started firing at us, one of the Serbs who brought us there. Then I hid behind a rock that was right below the house. When he stopped shooting then we started running through this valley by the house. It was full of bushes, shrubs, and then he was running and then he stumbled over and then I stumbled over him and then if I'd fall, then he'd run over me, but he was the first one to get out of that valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How long did you go on running?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Well, that is actually about 10 or 15 metres, that valley, that is, that's its diameter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is something that you can cover in two leaps, witness, so how did you manage to stumble and walk over each other so many times?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Well, that's what you can do if it's clear, but I've already told you that there were lots of bushes and shrubs there so it wasn't a road. It was a forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you left that valley and you went where?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: When I got out of the valley, this Muharem, well, he had already started running, he got out of the valley, and then there was a meadow that was a clearing of about 200 metres, no woods there, and then he ran, he started running, at that moment I saw that one of these Serbs walked around this valley. It was clear there. So he went around and he started firing after the man who had fled. I thought that I should flee too. But then I thought that I wouldn't stand a chance of running away because they would hit me. Then he emptied his magazine, and then I jumped into the valley again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you say that you heard what was going on in the house, right? You fled in the direction opposite the door, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Well, the door wasn't exactly on the opposite side. It was -- it was on the side, in relation to where I was in the valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what did you hear then, what was Karanovic saying to them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: It wasn't only Karanovic who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There were four of them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: There were four of them and they were making them go out and they were telling them to stand by the wall with their hands up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm a bit perplexed by that too, witness. How did they manage to drive them out when they had already been outside?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Not all of them. Not everybody was outside. I've already said that perhaps five of us were in a room. Some were still standing at the door. And others were outside. Now, whether they came in as well, I don't know. I have no way of seeing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. That means that they should have entered the room where the grenade had exploded?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: It's possible that they entered the room where I had been. Those people who were by the door. Maybe those people who were outside also went in to the place where the grenade had exploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what happened then? Was anybody wounded by this grenade?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: That, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you heard them being taken out, and you heard them shooting, and then bringing them inside again, into the house, that is?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Yes. I heard them saying, "This one is heavy. He weighs like 100 kilos." Things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, how can you claim that this grenade was not thrown by a Muslim thus leading to this catastrophe?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Are you saying that we tried to kill ourselves? Or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not trying to say that you wanted to kill yourselves but you did want to kill these four Chetniks. Not you from the inside but the others who were outdoors because you said that the grenade had come from outside, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Well, yes. Out there, in front of the entrance door. I believe it came from there. There was no other possibility because that house was a very old house, it was boarded up, and there was just this one room where that person used to live before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you went to Tomina, after Tomina you spent a month in Krings, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These four men, did they brag about this? Did they inform anyone about this?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: What do you mean, inform who?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These people who took you to Krings, did they inform anyone about what they had done?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: That, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you inform any authorities about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This Muharem is mentioned in relation to that exhumation as well. However, you know that he fled. Also you heard that he was arrested later on, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How come he's on that list, then, the exhumation list?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: You'll have to ask the person who wrote up that list. Probably since there is a memorial plaque there on the spot, that was erected by the relatives of the victims, then his name was included too. Now, whether this person wrote the list on the basis of that memorial plaque taking the names from the memorial plaque book, that's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have page 4 of this statement now? The one that's here right now, that is. In case of an exhumation, does one write the names that are found on a list or does one write the names of persons who had been identified? How can that kind of list include the name of a man who was not killed there? I think it's the one before this, the page before this. Maybe it's all right in English but I think in Serbian we need the previous page. How do you explain that? How do you explain that on the list of exhumed persons you find the name of a man who did not lose his life there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: I don't know who wrote the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'll just make the observation that it's not for the witness to comment on why somebody writes something down in an exhumation report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But he's talking about the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I misunderstood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see this here, where the name of this gentleman is mentioned? I don't want to mention it.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: On this page that is here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this statement, did you say that he had fled, that he had not lost his life there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: I'd have to read the statement again to see whether I had stated that he had fled from that spot, and that is what I kept saying all the time because it's the truth. He fled from that spot, the place where that house is. He fled from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's check out whether you mentioned that he fled at the time, but could you confirm that he is here as having been killed and burned on that place? Do you see his name or not? We can collapse the English page and zoom in on the B/C/S version, in particular I think his name appears in the sixth line from the bottom. Or around there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please zoom out a bit perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's, as I understand it, a different Muharem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's something the witness should tell us. Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's on the sixth line from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Yes, I can see his name here. Yes, it's Muharem Kenjar. He was born, it's possible that he was born in 1966 but as you can see most of these people had similar names, Muharem, Mehmed, son of this or that man. So there was always confusion about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the name of the man who had fled?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Safet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see below this stamp here that it says, son of Safet?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Well, I can't really read it. I can't make it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can't see the S and the A? And the F? Could we just zoom in on the stamp itself? The Tribunal's stamp. Yes, that's the one. Can you make out SAF?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Well, I can see the S but as for the rest, I'm not sure. It is possible that that's what it states there. It may be an error or something but I am still -- I'm still saying that this Muharem had fled and that later on he was seen in Sanski Most and then after that all track is lost of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How far was this Blazevic house from Kijevci?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: From where we were, about four kilometres perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you managed to walk that distance in how long?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Well, we were taken there one day, and we managed to get to Juric's house in about half -- in 30 minutes or half an hour. We stayed there the whole day and then on the next day we walked again for about half an hour or maybe even less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't need this document any more. Witness, sir, while you were in Tomina, you said that there were two kinds of men. One group were prisoners of war and the other were refugees, correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Well, I don't understand your question. I never said anything like that. I didn't mention prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, how were you treated and how were the others treated?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Well, we who had come from these two villages mentioned earlier, who came to Tomina, we were refugees. As for the rest, they were hosts there, they were locals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that you had spent the night in a house of a Muslim, I don't want to mention his name, that you found your mother there or his mother there, they fed you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And they told you that Muslim refugees from Hrustovo and Vrhpolje were accommodated there and that there were men there as well?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you say Chetniks came and took you away.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Some police and military personnel came. They used a bull horn. They were saying that everyone, all refugees, should come out and get on the main road and wait there, stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then the men whom they considered to be combatants, they took them away to Krings?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: No. We were all taken to Krings. Men, women, grown-ups, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when were women and children released?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: They were transported in the morning on buses and trucks. Later on, I learned that they were taken to Gracanica. You know where that is in Central Bosnia, near Doboj or whatever, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who were you interrogated by in Krings?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: By a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did he question you about?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Well, he asked me -- he told me to tell him everything, from the day the conflict broke out, up until that moment, to tell him my whereabouts, what I did, whether I had any weapons and so on. And whether I knew who had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many times were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Once.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was he writing anything down?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And on the basis of what you told him, you were released on 4 August, correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While some were sent to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Some people were taken to Manjaca as soon as we were brought in there, on that same morning, the women, the children and the elderly and infirm were transferred, they were taken away, whereas a group was sent to Manjaca either on the same day or the following day, I'm not quite sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there two judges in Sanski Most by the name of Adil Draganovic, or is there one man alone by that name?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: I believe there is only one man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know to what extent he was involved in the preparations for armed conflict in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Draganovic for the first time on the day when I provided the statement. What he did before that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you find it a bit unusual that he would investigate or question about matters that he participated in himself?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you mean. He did not take part in these events where I was involved. He wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement provided to him in 1996, it says that you came there on your own, without being summoned. How is it that you spoke about those matters for the first time then?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Because I was not in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the outcome of this battle in Hrustovo which lasted about two or three days, do you know how many dead, how many dead there were on either side?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Well, I didn't at the time. I learned later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did you find out?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: That there were many casualties, there were a lot of civilians killed in Hrustovo, in Vrhpolje, that one or two Serb soldiers were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that's what you've learned?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were not beaten in Krings by anyone, correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Yes. I was not beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that you weren't beaten harshly, that you weren't beaten much?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Well, yes, compared to the other prisoners, I was not mistreated too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you allowed at first to receive visitors by your relatives and to be brought some foodstuffs by them, but -- and that those visits were only banned later on but you were still -- you were still allowed to get food from outside, correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Yes. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please bear with me. I have to make selection here of what I'm going to skip. What did you know about paramilitary units? You mentioned some Serb defence forces or something. Did you know anything about paramilitary forces in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: I'm not sure what paramilitary units you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, what did you know about the military units that were there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: I knew that there were a lot of reservists and that there were a lot of armed Serbian soldiers, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These were reservists until the time when the Army of Republika Srpska was established, correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They were JNA reservists?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: That's possible. I know that they were there. I mean the JNA did not even exist any more at the time. It was abolished earlier, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the JNA left Bosnia on 9 May, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Maybe the JA, the Yugoslav army, but the NA, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree, then, that the Army of Republika Srpska was already in existence on 20 May and that these reservists of the Yugoslav army or the JNA at that time ceased being JNA reservists, they became reservists of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Do you mean as of 20 May and onwards?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Well, I believe that those units had become a Serb army long before that because there weren't any Muslims or Catholics in their ranks. There were just Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Serb forces, you're talking about the composition, right, but was the Army of Republika Srpska in existence before 20 May?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For planning purpose, I take it you do not have much for your re-examination, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Less than five minutes, I would think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have something?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, your time was up five minutes ago. Please conclude in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, do you know that the police in Sanski Most, the Serb police in Sanski Most, documented each incident and prosecuted them during the war and if it hadn't managed to do it during the war it did that after the war, all these prosecutions were conducted pursuant to investigations that had been conducted by Serbs during the war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Draganovic found at least 30 criminal prosecutions of Serbs who had committed something against Muslims?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, wouldn't it be -- wouldn't it have been appropriate for you to report what had happened at the Banovic house so that it could be documented and investigated by an investigating team?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: I don't think that would have been appropriate. I think that Muharem perhaps, who had fled the scene, that he would have been able to perhaps say something to the police and explain it. Had I tried to do that, the same would have happened to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, sir, we have a lot of documents that we cannot show today, where we see that Muslims approached freely went to the courts and submitted their criminal complaints and that these are still being prosecuted to this day. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. But as I'm out of time, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Witness, earlier this afternoon, Mr. Karadzic put to you, after the fighting in Hrustovo did you actually find shelter, and went on a little more and then you said it was into the second day of the fighting that you were invited to move into a certain place. And then just a moment ago, Mr. Karadzic also asked you -- he referred to the battle in Hrustovo. Do you recall both of those questions from Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall, when you testified in the Brdjanin case, and this is at transcript page 8053 and 8054, when you were asked about -- first of all, when there was a -- you were asked -- there was an announcement to hand over the weapons, and then you were asked in any point in May was Hrustovo shelled and you said yes. Was it before or after the announcement to hand over the weapons? You said to a slight degree before the announcement and then afterwards it was continued. Do you recall saying that in -- when you were asked in your evidence in the Brdjanin case? Giving that answer?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-052
utterances.text: Well, I can say this: I can't recall what he said in the other case but I will tell you as I recall the events themselves. First, the fighting broke out. Then the shelling started of Hrustovo. And then a day or two later, there was the announcement on the radio that weapons should be surrendered. That whoever had a weapon should surrender it and would be allowed to leave the town. In other words, to be able to get away from the combat zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, when you referred to the continued fighting, were you -- were you referring -- what were you referring to? Were you referring to that or the continued shelling?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is really a leading question and it is just putting pressure on the witness. The witness has already given an answer. Perhaps not to their liking but there is no need to seek another one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can ask him this way. You said that after the fighting in Hrustovo, you found shelter with your relative, we can say that in public. So what did you mean by "fighting"? And you also said in your answer that it was into the second day of the fighting that you found shelter. And you also said the fighting continued after that. So what did you mean by that word "fighting"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean after I left Hrustovo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will leave it in your hands. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No. Before, when you said that you went to your relative's place in Hrustovo, after the fighting, my question was, are you referring to -- what do you mean by the fighting? Are you referring to the shelling of Hrustovo which you mentioned in your prior testimony --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a reference? And could we please ask the Prosecutor to abstain from leading the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's on transcript page 8053.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, no. I asked the question. I asked the witness to clarify the meaning of "fighting" which he referred to. So it was before you left. So what did you mean by "fighting"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I meant the Muslims were shooting from one side and the Serbs from the other. This was how it was at the beginning. At first, it was with light weapons, perhaps there were one, two or three shells that landed. I don't know who fired them. But then some half day later or so, the shelling of Hrustovo started, and this was the Serb army shelling it. And this shelling went on for the whole day. And then on the next day, around noon time, there was a lull. And then came this announcement on the radio that all weapons should be surrendered and that afternoon there was no shelling any more. In other words, it was on that afternoon that I found shelter with my relative. At that time there was no shelling. But then a few days later, it got even worse, and I don't know much about that. All I could hear is the blasts, and I don't know who and how much shelling there was, but I do know one thing: There were no heavy weapons in Hrustovo. If anybody did have any weapons, that would be just light weapons, personal weapons. And also, in addition to that, I could see above Tomina village which is where the Serb positions were, I could see shells being fired. There was some artillery there. We could see flashes from the barrels and then -- from those positions, and then later on, a few moments later, we would hear the shell hitting Hrustovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are two associated exhibits for which numbers will be assigned. The first is 65 ter number 19922 which will be Exhibit P3377 under seal. And the second will be 19921 which will be Exhibit P3378 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber and the Tribunal, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it again. Now you are free to go, and please have a safe journey back home. We will take break for half an hour and resume at -- no, I'm sorry, for an hour, and resume at 1.40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Please take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Ms. Elliott?

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Can I please call up 65 ter number 22584 and e-court page 36.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: What's going to come up on the screen, Mr. Panic, is a transcript of your testimony in the Stanisic and Zupljanin proceedings on 11 to 13 November 2009. This is referring to page T-2902, at line 21, the transcript records the name "Milan Radic" and I understand from speaking with you that this should read, Milan Radovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, you've listened to your testimony in your own language. Was the information you provided to the Court accurate, and if you were asked the same questions today, would you provide the same information?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: May the transcript be admitted as the next exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3380, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask why the agreed practice has been abandoned of presenting an amalgamated statement? Is the OTP also suffering from time pressure or what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think there is any violation or inconsistency in admitting one statement. If the -- what was ordered was that if the OTP is minded to tender various statements, it should produce one amalgamated statement. However, in this case, they are going to tender just one transcript of testimony. Yes, Ms. Elliott.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: I'll read the 92 ter summary. Mr. Panic was the assistant commander for the reserve police station in Zvornik in 1992. On 6 April 1992, upon the order of police commander Dragan Spasojevic, the Serb police in Zvornik separated from the multi-ethnic police force. When they arrived at Alhos building in Karakaj, Dragan Spasojevic, Brano Grujic and some of Arkan's and Seselj's men were already there. On 8 April 1992, the action to take over Zvornik began. Arkan's unit led the action and the police were ordered to follow them and guard certain facilities. There was no serious resistance from the Muslim side. During this operation, Mr. Panic saw approximately five bodies dressed in civilian clothes. Various paramilitary units operated in Zvornik, including units under Zuca, Crni, Niski, Pivarski, Milorad Gogic and Simo Chetnik as well as the White Eagles. Several of these units were involved in moving women and children out of Muslim villages and detaining the men. Some paramilitary units were paid by the municipality or the MUP. On 1 June 1992, the Zvornik police commander at the time, Marinko Vasilic, ordered Mr. Panic and other police officers to Bijeli Potok where they assisted VRS units to load Muslims from the area of Klisa on to trucks and buses. Approximately 5.000 to 6.000 women, children and elderly men were put on buses and taken out of the area while approximately 700 men were taken to Karakaj Technical School. The Karakaj Technical School was guarded by the Karakaj Company. A few days later, Mr. Panic heard that the men from the Technical School were being executed at Gero's slaughterhouse. The police official who ran the reserve police station in Celopek reported to Mr. Panic that Muslims from Divic who were detained at the Celopek Dom Kulture were being killed and abused by a group led by Repic. Detention facilities in Zvornik including the Ekonomija farm, Ciglana and Celopek Dom Kulture were guarded by the Zvornik police. That completes the summary, Your Honour. If I can call up 65 ter number 00669, page 1 in the B/C/S and page 3 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: While this document is coming on to the screen, Mr. Panic, in your previous testimony, and this is at T-2872 for the Court's reference, you have named the Crisis Staff members of the Zvornik Crisis Staff. I'm not asking you to name them, but -- at this point but were these members generally associated with a particular political party?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, as far as the Serbian people were concerned, there was only the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Looking at the document on the screen, were you aware of the establishment of an interim government in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: And did many members also belong to the SDS?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: If I can go to page 2 in the B/C/S and page 5 in the English, please? What I'm referring you to, Mr. Panic, is the order on general mobilisation and my question is: Did this mobilisation take place?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: What measures were taken to implement the mobilisation order?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: People who did not respond to the mobilisation call-up were taken into custody by the military and the civilian police. And sometimes even the paramilitaries brought them in by force. So Pivarski and Niski went around the village and detained people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just correct the transcript? I think the witness said something like, "They took people off." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They stripped people, walked them around villages, and then they took them to detention facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. May this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3381, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: I'd ask that we go to Sanction, please. And I'm going to ask that Exhibit P2002 be played, without the sound.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: If we can pause, this is not the correct exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Yes, we just paused it at 11 seconds in the exhibit. Mr. Panic, do you recognise this location?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: This is a hamlet called Hrid in Zvornik, below Jedrinje. On the other side of the river is Mali Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are at .000516.6. Not 11 seconds. If you could confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Yes. This is a clip from a larger video so I think it's both but I can use that designation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: After the word "Zvornik" in the previous answer, the witness said, "Below is the Drina River."

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: If we can carry on playing the clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, do you recognise any of these individuals?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I think the man in the sheepskin coat, stout, is Milan Radovic, who used to work in the public utilities company. He drove a truck and collected dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: For the record, I've stopped at 531.8. If we could carry on playing the video, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, do you recognise this building?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: This is the SUP building in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: How about this -- the person that's in this picture? Are you able to tell us anything about this person?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Judging by the uniform, it's one of Arkan's men, and if you look at his back, he might even be Arkan himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: And do you have any idea of what's happening here, what's being shown?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Arkan's unit went to Zvornik first with the others, and they took control of the SUP building and they were hoisting the flag probably to celebrate liberation. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: I'm done with this. Oh, for the record I've paused it here at five minutes 43.4 and I'm done with the video at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is this clip part of?

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: This is a clip that was footage taken by Mr. [Indiscernible] that was introduced through Martin Bell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The first part we saw was Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I believe from when we started playing the correct clip the first part where we saw the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I meant the incorrect part.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know what the incorrect part was. But the video we have just played is Exhibit P2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that's part of video that has already been admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, just following up on Arkan, do you have any information as to how he came to be involved in the -- what you described as the liberation of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: His unit came earlier, and it was put up in the spa called Radaljska Banja in the environs of Zvornik and I heard later that Dragan Spasojevic talked around that 300.000 Deutschmark had been paid for the arrival of that unit, so he came with his unit and stayed at Radaljska Banja and during the attack on Zvornik itself on 8 or 9 April, the unit was led by a man called Pejo because Arkan himself was not there at the time. He came later.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: And Arkan, and Arkan's men, what sort of reputation did they have at the time, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: He had the reputation of a bad-tempered man. His name alone put the fear of God in everyone. He had been involved in the war in Croatia, in all the disorders and unrests at football matches and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: What about the other paramilitary groups operating in Zvornik? Do you have any information about whether they were invited or supported by the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Well, whether they were invited or not, I wouldn't know, but I know that Gogic's men were called to come again in May, and they put on police uniforms. In the beginning, they were paid by the municipality. Later on by the police. Whereas Zuca's men were paid by the municipality. But I don't know who was invited or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: If I could call up 65 ter number 00635? Mr. Panic, looking at the document on the screen before you, what formation does this document relate to?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: This is Gogic's unit, but it was called in even before the conflict started, and you can see from this paper that the municipality paid them. More precisely, the national defence staff. However, in May, they were paid by the police station in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: May this document be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3382, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter number 07693 and page 2 in the B/C/S, page 2 also in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, are you familiar with this unit, and can you recognise any of the signatures on the document?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: This is a reconnaissance unit led by Zoran Alexic originally from Brasina in Zvornik municipality. And below in handwriting, it says, "To accounts, pay out 100.000, approved by the commander." And somebody's signature. Brano Grujic, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: May this document be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In its entirety, I take it there is no objection. It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3383, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: May I please have 65 ter 15660 on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, were you aware that this group was in Zvornik and receiving support by the Serbian municipality?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I heard that White Eagles had been put up in Snagovo village which is in Zvornik municipality too but I didn't know about this certificate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: May this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think based on what the witness just said, I don't think that's a sufficient foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you recognise Mr. Grujic's signature? Mr. Panic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's typewritten, Branko Grujic but somebody else signed for him, as far as I can make out, it's Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you know who he is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know which Lazarevic it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You will have another opportunity to tender this, Ms. Elliott.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: May I please call up 65 ter 13934?

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: And while this document is coming up on the screen, Mr. Panic, I just want to ask you a clarification from your testimony, your prior testimony. And in that testimony you described a man from Seselj's unit beating a police colleague of yours because you and your colleagues were wearing your JNA caps with the five-pointed star. So my question has two parts: Did paramilitary units wear the JNA cap? And if not, what was their issue with it, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Paramilitary units did not wear the five-pointed star. In the former state of Yugoslavia, the five-pointed star was worn by the regular army and the police. Paramilitaries didn't. They had emblems depicting the eagle, the Serbian eagle, that we put on caps, and when we took them off later and replaced them again with the five-pointed star, he was so bitter about it he wanted to beat up a colleague with his truncheon because he had put on again the five-pointed star.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Turning your attention to the document before you on the screen, which is an Eastern Bosnia Corps report on the problems of Captain Dragan's training centre dated 7 June 1992, are you able to comment, Mr. Panic, comment on the issues surrounding the establishment of Captain Dragan's training centre in Divic?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Captain Dragan came sometime around the end of May. He arrived in Zvornik then. That was 1992. As for this decision, I did not know about that before, but I heard then that he wanted to establish a centre at the Vidikovac hotel in Divic but the municipal authorities did not agree and did not consent. But I heard that the army agreed to that and he opened it for a month or two. There was training up there in Divic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: May this document be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, I don't think that this document other than the witness's knowledge of Captain Dragan and where he was operating has been sufficiently confirmed by the witness and I point your attention, call your attention in the document to the part, portion, which states that Captain Dragan stated that he has the support of the president of the Presidency, Mr. Radovan Karadzic, and other ministers in the government of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and we don't think that a document with this assertion ought to be admitted for all purposes when the witness can only say that Captain Dragan had a centre at a certain location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to respond, Ms. Elliott?

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Well, I think the witness confirmed more than the mere existence of the centre. He confirmed that the centre was set up, that it was set up against the wishes of the municipal authorities, and I think there is sufficient connection to this document. In respect of the reference to Mr. Karadzic, we are about to see another document which is already in evidence that contains similar information. So I don't think that should be a barrier to admitting the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the Chamber has a basis to admit this, in light of the witness's confirmation of the existence of the training centre as well as the -- its relation with the Eastern Bosnia Corps, but with respect to that passage in question, the Chamber will emphasise that it will give no weight in the absence of any corroborating evidence at the moment. On that basis this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3384, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: If I can call up Exhibit P1478, and this is a portion of the Mladic notebooks so I'd like the B/C/S transcript, not the handwritten notebook, but the B/C/S transcript, e-court page 268 and English page 270.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, what's going to come up on the screen is 30 June 1992 entry that we looked at a few days ago, and while we are on the subject of the training centre, I'm going to direct your attention to remarks attributed to Mr. Karadzic, and then I'll go back to the beginning of that entry. So again, the e-court page is 268 in B/C/S and 270 in English. And I'm directing your attention to the comments of Mr. Karadzic to the effect that it would be a shame to abolish the centre. My question for you, Mr. Panic, is did Captain Dragan continue to operate the training centre after this time, which is 30 June 1992, and if so, do you know until when?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I don't know until when he had that centre, but I see here that a person called Crni is mentioned. He came from Teslic, and was attached to the police station at Zvornik and later on he went to Captain Dragan to Divic. I don't know exactly at what time the centre was closed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Do you know whether it was operating after 30 June 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: No. I've already said I don't know the date until which it operated.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Not the exact date, sir, but do you have any indication of the time period until which it operated, approximately?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I seem to remember that Captain Dragan stayed for about two months, two and a half months. He came at the end of May after Slavko Eric was killed. I think that he worked some more but I don't know until when.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can go to B/C/S page 244, English page 246. Mr. Panic, do you recognise the names of any of the participants at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Number 13, Jovo Mijatovic. Number 14, Radosav Peric.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: And what were their functions within Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Jovo Mijatovic was an MP. He worked in Glinica before the war. Radosav Peric was the principal of the school and later on he was Prime Minister in Zvornik, at the beginning of the war. And Vasilic, Slobodan, he was deputy commander of the brigade in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: If we could go over to the next page in both languages, please? Under the number 18, there are some more names listed. Do you recognise any of these individuals?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Marko Pavlovic. That's how he introduced himself there. He was commander of the staff of the Territorial Defence. However, later on, after he was tried as well as the group from Zvornik, that that is not his name; Gordan Jovanovic, a lawyer from Zvornik, he worked in the municipality previously; Tomasevic, Slavoljub, he worked in Glinica; then Grujic, Branko, that's the president of the municipality and president of the party; then Dragan Jokic is a military man, now, was he a captain or something. That is probably the composition of the staff of the Territorial Defence because it says chief up here by the name of Marko Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Can I go to B/C/S page 247, English page 249, please? I think we have English on both of them. If I could have the B/C/S page 249, please? Sorry, that's not the correct B/C/S page, sorry. It should be 247. My apologies. Yes, thank you. I'm directing your attention, Mr. Panic to where we have Mr. Grujic, this is at point number 4, reporting about the successful implementation of the president's decision, and my first question is: What happened to the inhabitants of Divic and Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Most of the inhabitants were relocated. Olovsko -- Municipality of Olovo was the place where the people of Divic were taken and Gornji Sepak, Subotica, Serbia and then Hungary.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: What about the inhabitants of Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I've already said the inhabitants of Kozluk were taken to Serbia. They stayed in Subotica, that's what I heard and then went to Hungary.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: And the inhabitants of Divic and Kozluk, were these Muslims?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: These places are primarily inhabited by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: And after the Muslims were relocated, were -- who settled in Divic and Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Persons of Serb ethnicity who had fled from their homes in Vogosca, Zenica and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: If I can go to B/C/S page 249, and English page 251? I'm just showing you this page, Mr. Panic, to show you that we have Marko Pavlovic speaking and you've already told us about him. So now if I can go to B/C/S page 251, English page 253 for a continuation of his comments? And I'm directing your attention to the bottom of this page, where

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVLOVIC IS REPORTING
utterances.text: [As read] "We were most active in evicting the Muslims. We had" -- and I'll ask that we go to the next page in both languages, please. And continuing on: [As read] "We had brought peace to Sepak, Divic and Kozluk. Some of them wanted to move out, while we demanded it. We had to evict some of the people also for the sake of our heroes who fled from Kovacevici." My first question is you've told us about Divic and Kozluk. What happened to the inhabitants of Sepak?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: There are three Sepaks: Donji, Gornji, and Srednji. Gornji and part of Srednji were mostly inhabited by Muslims and they moved to Serbia and I don't know where they went after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wonder whether the translation is correct here "evict." "[In English] We had to evict some of the people."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see the previous page? I didn't find the passage myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: It's at the very bottom of the previous page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not in the bottom part. It's up a bit. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: The reference to evict is, yes, the last star point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's an incorrect translation too. English cannot be justified by English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. That's the -- that's something that should be taken up on a separate moment, but not at the moment. Let's continue, Ms. Elliott.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: My next question, Mr. Panic, is are you able to comment on the reference Mr. Pavlovic made to the "heroes" from Kovacevici? Do you know what he would be referring to there?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Well, he probably meant persons of Serb ethnicity who had fled from the Muslims in Kovacevici, and then the -- they would move into those areas because Kovacevici was a predominantly Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: If I can call up 65 ter 17273, please? And while this document is coming up on the screen, Mr. Panic, can you provide an estimate as to when the process of moving out the Muslims from the Serbian Municipality of Zvornik was completed?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you the date, but it was right in the beginning, and then ended towards the end of June. I cannot give you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Looking at the document before you, were you aware of abandoned property being seized by the temporary government in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. The property of ethnic Muslims who had moved out was distributed to persons who were ethnic Serbs and who had moved in from other areas. This was done by a commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: The document before us on the screen isn't the correct page. Is this page 1 of the B/C/S and the English? And this is 17273? Yes, so instead of the right-hand side, I'll need the -- sorry, the right-hand side of the document enlarged. Yes, and on the basis of the witness's evidence, I'd ask that this document be marked as the next exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3385, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: If I can call up P03187, P3187, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: And while this is coming up on the screen, Mr. Panic, this is a map that you looked at in a larger print form when we met, and I'm turning now to a different subject, which is the detention facilities that you describe in your prior testimony. Mr. Panic, does this map with the photographs accurately depict those facilities, the facilities described there?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Except that there is Novi Izvor Ciglana here and then there was also the administration building and the misdemeanours court, in addition to all of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Just to clarify, what you refer to as the Ciglana is also what's recorded here as the Novi Izvor company; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Novi Izvor Ciglana is a factory where bricks are manufactured and tiles. Novi Izvor is a company, this is in Karakaj, but their main administration building was in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: What you refer to as the Ciglana, do you see a picture of that on this map? Can you see a picture of the Ciglana?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The first photograph, up here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps we could zoom in on what's the -- the photograph depicts that depicts what's called there the Novi Izvor company. It's got -- is this the photograph you're referring to? It bears the number 00406537.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is Ciglana, Novi Izvor. It is a factory that manufactures bricks and tiles so that is not their administration building. This is the actual factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: So the administration building that you refer to, and also misdemeanour court, that's a separate facility that's not shown on this map; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: That's a separate facility that is in Zvornik. It was secured by the police, whereas at the factory, Ciglana, the police did not secure that. This camp was founded by a paramilitary unit and later on it was abolished. But the police did secure the administration building in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. If I can call up 65 ter 14642, please? Mr. Panic, were you aware that there was TO command at Ekonomija at the time of this document?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I know that for a while the Territorial Defence -- a unit of it, not the command -- headed by Miladin Mijatovic who was a reserve captain of the army, was stationed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: May this document be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I really question whether this witness has given a sufficient basis for admission of this document, simply on the fact that the unit -- a unit was located at a certain place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view, on the basis of the witness's evidence, we can admit this unless you challenge the authenticity of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we note that the people who received it haven't -- there is no signatures of the people that received it so it may not be a complete document but we don't challenge the authenticity of this document per se.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will give it a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3386, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Now turning, Mr. Panic, to a couple of questions about the Karakaj Technical School, in your prior testimony you talked about the execution of men from the school at the slaughterhouse. How did you hear about that? Where did you get that information from?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I heard of that in a conversation with police officer Petar Tanic, who secured the commission for sanitisation, and on one occasion he told me that he had to go to the slaughterhouse in order to secure the bodies of the ethnic Muslims who had been held at the Technical School and who had been slaughtered there but there was also talk about it, there were rumours in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: And how about at the school itself? Did you hear whether any killings took place at the Karakaj Technical School?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Well, it was rumoured that paramilitary units, Pivarski, Repic came, went there and that they mistreated and beat the people there but whether they killed them or not I really wouldn't know because I did not go to the technical centre. There were all kinds of stories, but I didn't see any of it so I couldn't really say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever see Milan Radovic around the Karakaj Technical School around June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. One day as I was passing, going over the overpass in Karakaj, I saw that there was a municipal truck driven by Milan Radovic at that time, leaving the premises, but what it was that he was transporting, I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm moving to my final topic. In your prior testimony, you spoke of seven policemen who were sentenced in Sarajevo for these war events and the reference is T-2934. When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I think that they were sentenced last year, and that they are serving their terms. These people had been guards at the administration building in Novi Zvornik during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: And at the time, and by that I mean in 1992, were you involved in or aware of any investigations into abuses at any of the detention facilities in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: In the early days of the war operations, I don't think there were any investigations conducted. I just know that doctors, pathologists, came to examine, to carry out examinations, but later on I know that in a report that was submitted by the chief of police.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the name.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I saw that there were three criminal complaints against three individuals for war crimes and one criminal complaint for rape. Now, this report was drafted sometime either on 7 or 9 January 1993, and the report referred to the period 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: And were you personally involved in any of these investigations?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. That completes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we deal with the associated exhibits you are going to tender?

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Now there is only seven of them. A number of them have been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Are there any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you take a look at 65 ter 18479, which was referred to in transcript page 2935? If you could explain to me how it was -- it forms an inseparable and indispensable part of this transcript?

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: I believe the witness commented that he was familiar with the author of this document and his position as well as that he was generally aware that Zuco had been released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he said -- he identified the author and that's it. If you could deal with this document, if you would like to tender it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Yes. If I can call up 18479, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Witness, looking at the document before you on the screen, were you aware that Zuco had been disarmed on 29 July 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, the Special Police came and not only disarmed but also arrested Zuco's unit, and on the days prior to that, the 27th and 28th, we managed to expel Gogic and his men across the bridge and into Mali Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: And you mentioned that Zuco was arrested. Do you know what happened to him after his arrest?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: They were all escorted to Bijeljina. What happened after that, I really don't know. I did see him later on. He married a woman from Celopek, and he came there so I could -- I saw him, I had occasion to see him. But I don't know what happened with the trial or the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Did you know at -- or did you hear at some point in time that he had been released?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was released, because I saw him on a number of occasions later on. He moved around our area. And later on he was also arrested in Belgrade on a couple of occasions, and I heard that there too he would then be released.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure if that's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's a sufficient basis. Thank you, Ms. Elliott. Including that part the seven associated exhibits, all of them, will be admitted and given number in due course. Thank you, Ms. Elliott. We have some ten minutes, Mr. Karadzic. Can you start on some introductory part? Yes, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, can you leave me about two minutes, if we could make an oral response to the Prosecution's motion for leave to reply to a document relating to the ICMP. Before we recess if I could have about two minutes to give you an oral response to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Panic.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to use what little time is left to us to clarify some of your words of today. When you say that Zuco was released, does that mean that the proceedings against him have been -- had ended or that he was -- that he had served his sentence and left, that it was still ongoing?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know. He was released but whether the proceedings against him were still in effect or ongoing, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was not properly interpreted. It doesn't mean that the proceedings were suspended but that he was probably released from detention, but the proceedings against him, whether they were still ongoing, I don't know. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, since both of you are speaking the same language, you need to put a pause between the question and answer. Please bear that in mind tomorrow. Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We saw that video insert where the two bodies were being carried out. Would you agree with me that it would be hard to determine, based on their clothes, what those two men were by ethnicity, and that the woman was probably a Serb woman?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I don't understand which two men you're referring to. Are you referring to the two men who were carrying the body or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, the two bodies. They were carrying a body of a man, and would you agree that we couldn't determine his ethnicity but would you also agree that the body of the woman, judging by her clothes, the clothing, it's probably a Serb woman? And I'm referring to the bodies.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really decide on anyone's ethnicity based on their clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever hear that some part owner, some of the owners of Glinica from Serbia were concerned about their investments and this factory had an output of up to $1 million per day and that they had to do something in order to pay for the protection of Glinica? Of Alumina?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Well, all I know is that Jefto Subotic, the former manager of Glinica, came to Glinica for some reason but why it was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the municipality have at their disposal 300.000 marks in order to pay out Arkan?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the municipality did not have those funds, but where they managed to get them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on page 67 that was shown earlier, relating to Captain Dragan, it says that he helped with equipping and training. Now, would you tell us, please, up to that point in time, did -- had Captain Dragan taken any part in any combat or did he only train men, those men who were referred from the brigade? Now, did he only -- was he only involved in training and did you ever hear of any crime that he had committed prior to that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Well, I know he didn't take part in the fighting. He arrived there sometime after 25 May, and from what I heard, it was in order to go to Kamenica village in order to pull out the body of -- the bodies of some men who were killed there. However, he then went to Zvornik, he walked about Zvornik, and I don't know. He did establish the centre but I don't know that he took part in any fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you don't know that he committed any crime?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Well, no, I don't really know. Maybe they engaged in robberies but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should we wrap up for the day or should I continue? There are three minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, probably yes. Mr. Panic, we will continue tomorrow at 9.00. Probably you have been told about this, but you are not supposed to discuss with anybody about your testimony. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you may be excused now. Please have a nice evening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, I take it we need to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I think this can be heard in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, this morning the OTP filed a request for leave to reply to the response to the Prosecution's request for further orders with respect to ICMP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On two points, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct. And I'd like to make an oral response so that you could make a timely ruling on it, if that's okay. It will just take a minute. Normally we don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Normally we don't object to requests. We think the parties ought to be free to make whatever replies they would like but I would just note in this particular instance given that we have not really taken an objection to the relief sought by OTP, that the reply really seems more in the nature of bickering among -- about some facts that aren't particularly of assistance to the Chamber. And so we oppose the request for leave to apply and ask you to just go ahead and decide the motion on what you have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, obviously, once that characterisation is made then any response there is going to be an attempt to shoehorn any response into the category of bickering. It's not. Where representations are made that the Prosecution believes need to be clarified so that the matter can proceed, on the basis of accurate information, we attempt to do so and that's all we have done here, Mr. President. We want to ensure that the record is kept straight and that the Trial Chamber can make the most appropriate decision based on the most accurate information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will consider the submissions. Yes, Mr. Harvey? Could you introduce your new member?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I apologise for not introducing earlier Ms. Sarah Codde who is a pro bono legal assistant working with my team. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Welcome, Ms. Codde. We will rise today and resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 20th day of September, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: [Private session] [Confidentiality partially lifted by order of Chamber]
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.00 p.m.,
